entries.title: ATTACK SURFACE
entries.body: Refers to the set of all potential entry points that an attacker can exploit to gain access to a system. The attack surface includes all the interfaces, services, ports, protocols, and other communication vectors that may be exposed. A larger attack surface increases vulnerabilities and therefore makes the system more likely to be attacked. Reducing the attack surface is a good security practice that involves disabling unnecessary services. For example, in the context of Bitcoin, *hardware wallets* have a much smaller attack surface than *software wallets*. Indeed, they isolate the keys on a device that is not connected to the Internet and has very few interfaces and services. In contrast, *software wallets* are installed on general-purpose PCs, which have a much larger attack surface because of the many features and network connections they support.

entries.title: BLIND SIGNATURE
entries.body:
Chaum's blind signatures are a form of digital signature in which the issuer of a signature does not know the content of the message they are signing. But the signature can then be verified against the original message. This technique was developed by the cryptographer David Chaum in 1983.

Take the example of a company wishing to have a confidential document, such as a contract, authenticated without revealing its content. The company applies a blinding process that cryptographically transforms the original document in a reversible way. This modified document is sent to a certification authority, which affixes a blind signature without knowing the underlying content. After receiving the signed blinded document, the company unblinds the signature. The result is an original document authenticated by the authority's signature, without the authority ever having seen the original content.

Chaum's blind signatures therefore make it possible to certify the authenticity of a document without knowing its content, which guarantees both the confidentiality of the user's data and the integrity of the signed document.

On Bitcoin, this protocol is found in Chaumian bank systems built as overlays (Cashu, Fedimint...), but above all in Chaumian coinjoin protocols, in order to ensure that the coordinator is not able to link an input to an output.

entries.title: BLIND SIGNING
entries.body: Process in which a user signs a Bitcoin transaction without being able to precisely verify the details of what they are signing. In the context of *hardware wallets*, blind signing is dangerous, because the user must rely on the connected computer to display the information (recipients, fees, amounts...). This exposes them to vulnerabilities, because the computer is connected to the internet and has a much larger attack surface than the signing device. If the computer is compromised, it can manipulate the displayed details and submit a malicious transaction for signing without the user being aware of it. To avoid this risk, it is recommended to use *hardware wallets* with a built-in screen, and to verify the information on it before signing transactions.

entries.title: BLOCK SUBSIDY
entries.body: The quantity of new units that can be created by the miner who solves a block. This subsidy is part of the block reward, along with transaction fees. It is distributed within a specific transaction called the “coinbase.” Initially set at 50 bitcoins per block in 2009, this subsidy is halved every 210,000 blocks (roughly every four years) through a process known as the “halving.” When the subsidy falls below the amount of 1 sat, it will no longer be possible to collect it, and the block reward will rely solely on transaction fees. Unless the protocol is modified, the circulating money supply will then no longer be able to increase.

entries.title: BOLTZMANN SCORE
entries.body:
Indicator used to evaluate the level of privacy of a Bitcoin transaction. The Boltzmann score is based on the number of possible interpretations of a transaction, that is, the number of plausible combinations between the *inputs* and the *outputs*.

The principle is inspired by the statistical physics of Ludwig Boltzmann: the more possible combinations (of microstates) a transaction admits, the higher its entropy, and the harder it is to analyze. The score is generally expressed in bits of entropy. A transaction with a score of 0 bits has only one possible interpretation (each *input* is clearly linked to an *output*). Conversely, a well-constructed *coinjoin* can reach a high score, because the multiple *inputs* and *outputs* of identical amounts generate a very large number of possible combinations.

This score allows users to objectively evaluate the effectiveness of a *coinjoin* or of any transaction in terms of privacy.

entries.title: CHECKSUM
entries.body:
A checksum is a value calculated from a set of data, used to verify the integrity and validity of that data during its transmission or storage. Checksum algorithms are designed to detect accidental errors or unintentional alterations of data, such as transmission errors or file corruption. Different types of checksum algorithms exist, such as parity checks, modular checksums, cryptographic hash functions, or BCH codes (*Bose, Ray-Chaudhuri and Hocquenghem*).

On Bitcoin, checksums are used at the application level to ensure the integrity of receiving addresses. A checksum is calculated from the payload of a user's address, then appended to that address in order to detect possible errors when it is entered. A checksum is also present in recovery phrases (mnemonic).

*It is generally accepted to use the English term "checksum" directly in French.*

entries.title: COIN SELECTION
entries.body: Process by which Bitcoin wallet software chooses which UTXOs to use as inputs to satisfy the outputs of a transaction. The coin selection method is important, because it has consequences for the cost of a transaction and the user's privacy. It often aims to minimize the number of inputs used, in order to reduce the size of the transaction and the associated fees, while trying to preserve privacy by avoiding merging coins from different sources (CIOH). Several methods exist for coin selection, such as the *Knapsack Solver* or *Branch-and-Bound*. When coin selection is done manually by the user, it is called “*Coin Control*”.

entries.title: DIGITAL SIGNATURE
entries.body: Cryptographic proof that demonstrates possession of a specific private key, associated with a unique public key, without having to disclose it. On Bitcoin, it is built using the private key and the hash of a transaction. It attests to ownership of the bitcoins concerned and makes it possible to satisfy a script that unlocks a UTXO. It is generated by means of an elliptic curve digital signature algorithm such as ECDSA or the Schnorr protocol.

entries.title: LARGEST OUTPUT
entries.body:
An internal chain analysis heuristic. When a sufficiently large gap is spotted between 2 transaction outputs in a simple payment pattern, one can estimate that the largest output is likely the change output. This largest output heuristic is probably the least precise of all. If identified on its own, it is quite weak. However, this characteristic can be combined with other heuristics in order to reduce the uncertainty of our interpretation.

![Largest output: an input of 451,458 sats yields 57,814 and 390,987, the gap suggesting a change output of 390,987.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LoicPandul/Dictionnaire-de-Bitcoin/bab568e32351cc9f1240f49f5feedc242123d101/definitions/fr/s/sortie-la-plus-grande/assets/image-1.png)

entries.title: LAYER
entries.body:
A protocol or network built on top of the main Bitcoin network, stacked above it. It uses the Bitcoin network as a foundation and is therefore dependent on its protocol. However, the Bitcoin network is not dependent on its layers. An example of such a layer is the Lightning Network.

These layers are designed to extend the capabilities of the Bitcoin network by adding additional features or capabilities, such as faster transactions, tokens or micropayments. They are often created to address certain limitations of the Bitcoin network, while benefiting from its security and decentralization. It is important to note that although these layers are built on the Bitcoin network, they have their own protocols and mechanisms, distinct from those of the Bitcoin network itself.

entries.title: SAMOURAI WALLET
entries.body:
Bitcoin wallet software for Android mobile devices, focused on privacy. It offers advanced features such as Whirlpool, Stonewall, StonewallX2, Ricochet and Stowaway (payjoin) coinjoins. Samourai also implements numerous protections to help users protect their privacy against chain analysis.

*On April 24, 2024, the two co-founders of Samourai Wallet were unjustly arrested for simply writing code. I want to express my unwavering support for them. Their commitment to privacy and freedom embodies the fundamental values of Bitcoin. These developers committed no crime; they only worked to offer tools allowing everyone to assert their natural rights. To support them in this ordeal, I invite everyone to sign the online petition: https://billandkeonne.org/.*

entries.title: SAT - SATOSHI
entries.body: The satoshi, often abbreviated as "sat", is the smallest subdivision of bitcoin that can be recorded on the blockchain. It is named in honor of the inventor of Bitcoin, Satoshi Nakamoto. A single bitcoin is divided into 100,000,000 sats, which means that one satoshi equals 0.00000001 bitcoin. Because of its small unit value, the sat is often used to set prices, particularly in small transactions. Its use is often preferred over BTC on the Lightning Network.

entries.title: SATOCHIP
entries.body:
Belgian company specialized in manufacturing hardware wallets (*hardware wallets*) in a smart card format. The main product, the Satochip, is an NFC card equipped with an EAL6+ certified secure element, which allows Bitcoin private keys to be stored securely.

The range also includes the SeedKeeper, a secure storage device for mnemonic phrases, and the Satodime, a physical bearer instrument for bitcoins. All the associated software is open source.

entries.title: SATODIME
entries.body: Bearer NFC card developed by Satochip, a Belgian company. The Satodime supports up to three independent "vaults" for storing bitcoins. The private keys are generated and sealed in an EAL6+ certified secure chip and are only revealed at the moment of unsealing, which means that physical possession of the card is equivalent to ownership of the funds.

entries.title: SATOSHIDICE
entries.body:
Bitcoin gambling website, launched in April 2012 by Erik Voorhees. The service operated as a probabilistic dice game: players sent bitcoins to addresses corresponding to different levels of winning probability, and automatically received a payment back according to the result. The site quickly dominated transaction activity on the Bitcoin blockchain. At its peak in 2012 and early 2013, it accounted for nearly half of the transactions recorded on the network.

In July 2013, Erik Voorhees sold the service for 126,315 BTC (approximately 12.4 million dollars at the time). In June 2014, the *Securities and Exchange Commission* (SEC) brought charges against Voorhees for the sale of unregistered securities, related to offerings of shares in SatoshiDice and FeedZeBirds to investors in 2012 and 2013. It is considered one of the first large-scale commercial services on Bitcoin.

entries.title: SATOSHILABS
entries.body: Czech company founded in 2013 by Marek Palatinus and Pavol Rusnák, known for having created the Trezor, the very first hardware wallet (*hardware wallet*) in history. Based in Prague, SatoshiLabs has also contributed to the development of important standards for the Bitcoin ecosystem, including BIP-0039, which defines mnemonic phrases.

entries.title: SATSCARD
entries.body: Bearer NFC card manufactured by Coinkite. The Satscard makes it possible to physically transfer bitcoins from hand to hand without an on-chain transaction at the time of the exchange. It contains 10 independent *slots*, each associated with a private key and a unique address: the bitcoins are loaded onto a *slot*, then "unsealed" by the recipient using a PIN code and a compatible application such as Nunchuk.

entries.title: SBI CRYPTO
entries.body: Bitcoin mining pool based in Tokyo, operated by SBI Crypto, a subsidiary of the Japanese financial group SBI Holdings. SBI Holdings has been mining on its own account since 2017, before opening its pool to the public in 2021. It is aimed at individual miners as well as professional operators.

entries.title: SCALABILITY
entries.body:
Refers to Bitcoin's ability to handle an increase in transaction volume while maintaining acceptable performance. Bitcoin faces inherent technical limitations, such as block size, the time interval between each block, and the fact that a transaction is only considered immutable after several confirmations. These constraints prevent Bitcoin from processing an unlimited number of transactions efficiently. When demand for block space intensifies, users are forced to increase the fees they offer so that their transactions are processed. Scalability, that is, Bitcoin's ability to handle the increase in transaction volume, can be improved either by direct changes to the protocol or by external solutions such as the Lightning Network. The question of scalability has always been at the heart of heated debates within the community. The first attempt to increase the block size dates back to October 2010 with [a patch proposed by Jeff Garzik](https://bitcointalk.org/index.php?topic=1347.0). It is this subject of scalability that notably led to the block size war between 2015 and 2017.

*The French term "scalabilité" is an anglicism. The proper French translation of the English term "scalability" is "évolutivité" or else "passage à l'échelle". However, it is generally accepted within the community to use the term "scalabilité" directly.*

entries.title: SCB - STATIC CHANNEL BACKUP
entries.body:
Backup mechanism introduced by LND that makes it possible to recover one's funds in the event of data loss on a Lightning node. The SCB is a file (generally named `channel.backup`, not to be confused with the file `channel.db`) that contains static information about open channels: the identity of peers, the means of contacting them and the channel identifiers.

Unlike the `channel.db` database, which changes with every payment, the SCB is only updated when a channel is opened or closed. It does not contain the detailed state of the channels or the transaction history. The SCB therefore does not make it possible to restore a Lightning node as it was: its role is to ask peers to force-close the channels in order to recover the funds *onchain*.

During a restoration, the user provides their aezeed seed (to recreate the *onchain* wallet) and the SCB file. LND then contacts each peer to notify them of the data loss. The peer broadcasts its latest commitment transaction to close the channel, and the funds reappear in the *onchain* wallet. This mechanism depends on the cooperation and availability of peers: if a peer is offline or uncooperative, the funds in the channel concerned may remain locked indefinitely.

entries.title: SCHEMA
entries.body: In the context of the RGB protocol, a Schema refers to a piece of declarative code that defines the set of variables, rules and business logic (*Business Logic*) governing the operation of a contract. It specifies the structure of the state, notably the initial configuration established during the Genesis, and details the types of transitions allowed as well as the strict conditions for their validation. The Schema serves as a normative framework, ensuring that any change to the contract's state conforms to the rules established by the developer of the Schema.

entries.title: SCHNORR PROTOCOL
entries.body: The Schnorr protocol is a digital signature algorithm based on elliptic curve cryptography (ECC). It is used on Bitcoin to derive a public key from a private key and to sign a transaction with a private key. On Bitcoin, just like ECDSA, Schnorr is based on the use of the elliptic curve `secp256k1`, characterized by the equation: `y^2 = x^3 + 7`. The Schnorr signature protocol has been implemented in the Bitcoin protocol since November 2021 with the activation of the Taproot upgrade.

entries.title: SCID - SHORT CHANNEL ID
entries.body:
Compact identifier used on the Lightning Network to uniquely reference a payment channel. Rather than using the public keys of the two nodes or the full txid of the funding transaction, the SCID encodes the exact position of the channel in the blockchain in a condensed format.

The SCID is made up of three elements concatenated over 8 bytes: the number of the block containing the funding transaction (3 bytes), the index of that transaction in the block (3 bytes), and the index of the output (*output*) corresponding to the channel (2 bytes). For example, an SCID `700000x1x0` means: block no. 700,000, transaction no. 1, output no. 0.

entries.title: SCORE BASED METHOD
entries.body:
Method of calculating miners' remuneration in the context of mining pools. This reward system is proportional, but weighted by the moment at which the *share* is submitted. The SCORE method values shares according to the time elapsed since the start of the mining cycle. The later a share is submitted in the cycle, the higher its value. This method makes it possible to encourage miners to stay, because each time the miner stops mining, their score stagnates while those of the others increase more and more quickly.

*This method is sometimes also called "Bitcoin Pooled Mining" (BPM).*

entries.title: SCRIPT
entries.body: Stack-based programming language used to establish spending conditions, and therefore, indirectly, to secure bitcoins. Script is essentially a list of instructions, made up of logical operators and commands to manipulate the stacks (*stacks*). It materializes through the use of opcodes that give specific instructions that are executed by nodes to verify the validity of a transaction. Script is a non-Turing-complete language. It can be categorized as a mid-level language (almost low-level) inspired by Forth.

entries.title: SCRIPTLESS SCRIPTS
entries.body: Concept initially developed by Andrew Poelstra that allows the execution of smart contracts without explicitly exposing the contract logic on the Bitcoin blockchain. As the name "scriptless script" suggests, the idea is based on executing scripts (or contracts) without explicitly resorting to scripts. These contracts exploit the properties of Schnorr signatures that allow the use of *Adaptor Signatures*, notably to carry out *Atomic Swaps*. The conditions of the contract are applied and executed off-chain by the parties involved, who are the only ones to know its terms. Unlike conventional smart contracts, *Scriptless Scripts* minimize their footprint on the blockchain, thus reducing the cost of the operation. These contracts are also more discreet than conventional smart contracts, which leave traces on the blockchain. They therefore look like ordinary transactions, which increases their anonset.

entries.title: SCRIPTPUBKEY
entries.body:
Script located in the output part of a Bitcoin transaction that defines the conditions under which the associated UTXO can be spent. This script therefore makes it possible to secure bitcoins. In its most common form, the `scriptPubKey` contains a condition requiring the next transaction to provide proof of possession of the private key corresponding to a specified Bitcoin address. This is often achieved by a script that requires a signature matching the public key associated with the address used to secure those funds. When a transaction attempts to use this UTXO as an input, it must provide a `scriptSig` that, once combined with the `scriptPubKey`, satisfies the conditions set and produces a valid script. 

For example, here is a classic P2PKH `scriptPubKey`:

```text
OP_DUP
OP_HASH160
OP_PUSHBYTES_20
<hash de la clé publique>
OP_EQUALVERIFY
OP_CHECKSIG
```

The corresponding `scriptSig` would be:

```text
<signature> <clé publique>
```

![Bitcoin transaction: the ScriptPubKey locks the output, the ScriptSig in the input provides the proof to unlock it.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LoicPandul/Dictionnaire-de-Bitcoin/bab568e32351cc9f1240f49f5feedc242123d101/definitions/fr/s/scriptpubkey/assets/image-1.png)

*To refer to this script, one sometimes also speaks of a "locking script" or "script de verrouillage" in French.*

entries.title: SCRIPTSIG
entries.body:
Element in a Bitcoin transaction located in the inputs. The `scriptSig` provides the data necessary to satisfy the conditions set by the `scriptPubKey` of the previous transaction whose funds are being spent. It therefore plays a complementary role to the `scriptPubKey`. Typically, the `scriptSig` contains a digital signature and a public key. The signature is generated by the owner of the bitcoins using their private key and proves that they have the authorization to spend the UTXO. In this case, the `scriptSig` demonstrates that the holder of the input possesses the private key corresponding to the public key associated with the address specified in the `scriptPubKey` of the previous outgoing transaction.

When the transaction is verified, the data of the `scriptSig` is executed in the corresponding `scriptPubKey`. If the result is valid, this means that the conditions for spending the funds have been fulfilled. If all the inputs of the transaction provide a `scriptSig` that validates their `scriptPubKey`, the transaction is valid and can be added to a block for its execution.

For example, here is a classic P2PKH `scriptSig`:

```text
<signature> <clé publique>
```

The corresponding `scriptPubKey` would be:

```text
OP_DUP
OP_HASH160
OP_PUSHBYTES_20
<hash de la clé publique>
OP_EQUALVERIFY
OP_CHECKSIG
```

![ScriptSig in the input with an open padlock and ScriptPubKey locking the output: the pair validates the spending of a UTXO.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LoicPandul/Dictionnaire-de-Bitcoin/bab568e32351cc9f1240f49f5feedc242123d101/definitions/fr/s/scriptsig/assets/image-1.png)

*The `scriptSig` is also sometimes called "unlocking script" or "script de déverrouillage" in French.*

entries.title: SCRIPTWITNESS
entries.body:
Element in the inputs of SegWit transactions that contains the signatures and public keys necessary to unlock the bitcoins sent in the transaction. Similar to the `scriptSig` of Legacy transactions, the `scriptWitness` is however not placed in the same location. Indeed, it is this part, called the "witness" ("*witness*" in English), that is moved into a separate data structure in order to solve the problem of transaction malleability. Each SegWit input has its own `scriptWitness`, and all the `scriptWitness` together form the `Witness` field of the transaction.

*Be careful not to confuse the `scriptWitness` with the `witnessScript`. While the `scriptWitness` contains the witness data of any SegWit input, the `witnessScript` defines the spending conditions of a P2WSH or P2SH-P2WSH UTXO and constitutes a script in its own right, in the manner of the `redeemScript` for a P2SH output.*

entries.title: SDK - SOFTWARE DEVELOPMENT KIT
entries.body:
Set of software tools providing the resources developers need to create applications on a specific platform. An SDK includes libraries, development guides, code examples or even build processes. SDKs make development easier and faster by offering reusable modules. On Bitcoin, there are the BDK (*Bitcoin Dev Kit*) and the LDK (*Lightning Dev Kit*).

*In English, SDKs are also sometimes called "devkit".*

entries.title: SE - SPARK ENTITY
entries.body:
Group of operators responsible for managing shared keys and signing operations within the Spark protocol. The SE collectively holds one half of the spending key associated with the UTXOs locked in Spark, the other half being held by the user. During a transfer on Spark, the SE participates in the renewal of the key shares: it destroys its share associated with the previous owner and generates a new one with the recipient, which makes the old share cryptographically unusable.

The SE is not a single entity but a set of independent *Spark Operators* (SO) that cooperate via a threshold signature protocol, based on Schnorr signatures. No individual operator possesses the complete key. The security model relies on a 1-of-n assumption: it is enough for a single SO to be honest to prevent any collusion with a previous owner. Trust is only required at the time of the transfer: once the old keys are destroyed, the operators can no longer affect the funds, even if they are compromised later.

entries.title: SEAL DEFINITION
entries.body: In the context of the RGB protocol, the Seal Definition is the component of an Assignment that explicitly links a commitment to a UTXO held by the new owner. It specifies the location of the state by identifying the UTXO with which it is associated, which formally establishes the ownership of an asset or a right on RGB.

entries.title: SECP256K1
entries.body:
Name given to a specific elliptic curve used in the Bitcoin protocol to implement the ECDSA (*Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm*) and Schnorr digital signature algorithms. The `secp256k1` curve was chosen by Bitcoin's inventor, Satoshi Nakamoto. It has certain interesting properties, notably advantages in terms of performance.

The use of `secp256k1` on Bitcoin means that each private key (a random 256-bit number) is mapped to a corresponding public key by point addition and doubling of the private key by the generator point of the `secp256k1` curve. This operation is easy to carry out in one direction, but practically impossible to reverse, which is the basis of the security of digital signatures on Bitcoin.

The `secp256k1` curve is specified by the elliptic curve equation `y^2 = x^3 + 7`, which means that it has coefficients `a` equal to `0` and `b` equal to `7` in the general form of the equation of an elliptic curve `y^2 = x^3 + ax + b`. `secp256k1` is defined over a finite field whose order is a very large prime number, specifically `p = 2^{256} - 2^{32} - 977`. The curve also has a group order, which is the number of distinct points on the curve, a predefined generator point (or `G` point), which is used in cryptographic operations to generate key pairs, and a cofactor that is equal to `1`.

*“SEC” stands for “Standards for Efficient Cryptography”. “P256” indicates that the curve is defined over a field `\mathbb{Z}_p` where `p` is a 256-bit prime number. “K” refers to the name of its inventor, Neal Koblitz. Finally, “1” indicates that it is the first version of this curve.*

entries.title: SECP256R1
entries.body:
Name given to an elliptic curve defined by the NIST standard for public-key cryptography. It uses a 256-bit prime field and an elliptic curve equation `y^2 = x^3 + ax + b` with the constants:

```text
a=-3
```

and 

```text
b=41058363725152142129326129780047268409114441015993725554835256314039467401291
```

The `secp256r1` curve is widely used in many protocols, but it is not used in Bitcoin. Indeed, Satoshi Nakamoto opted for the `secp256k1` curve, which was little known in 2009. The precise reason for this choice is unknown, but it may have been in order to minimize the risk of backdoors. The parameters of the `k1` curve are, in fact, significantly simpler than those of the `r1` curve, in particular the constant `b`.

*This curve is sometimes also called “P-256”.*

entries.title: SECPOOL
entries.body: Bitcoin mining pool oriented mainly toward the Asian and Russian-speaking market. SECPOOL offers FPPS and PPLNS payout methods.

entries.title: SECURE ELEMENT
entries.body:
Electronic chip resistant to physical attacks, designed to store sensitive data and run cryptographic operations in an isolated environment. In general computing, *secure elements* are found in bank cards, biometric passports, SIM cards and the TPM (*Trusted Platform Module*) modules of computers. They are designed to resist side-channel attacks (*side-channel attacks*), fault injection attacks and attempts at physical reverse engineering. *Secure elements* are generally certified under the international Common Criteria (CC) standard, with assurance levels ranging from EAL1 to EAL7.

In the context of Bitcoin, *secure elements* are used in *hardware wallets* to protect private keys against any unauthorized access, including in the event of physical compromise of the device. The private key is generated and stored inside the chip, and signing operations are performed internally without ever exposing the key outside the component. Most *hardware wallet* manufacturers integrate a *secure element* into their devices: Ledger (with ST chips from STMicroelectronics), Coldcard (with ATECC608 chips from Microchip), BitBox02, Trezor Safe (with the TROPIC01 chip) and others. Some devices such as Blockstream's Jade take an alternative approach called a *virtual secure element*, where the key is protected by a distributed encryption scheme rather than by a dedicated physical chip.

entries.title: SEED NODES
entries.body:
Static list of public Bitcoin nodes, built directly into the source code of Bitcoin Core (`bitcoin/src/chainparamsseeds.h`). This list serves as connection points for new Bitcoin nodes joining the network, but it is only used if the DNS seeds do not provide a response within 60 seconds of being queried. In that case, the new Bitcoin node will connect to these seed nodes to establish a first connection to the network and request IP addresses of other nodes. The ultimate goal is to acquire the information needed to perform the IBD and synchronize with the chain that has the most accumulated work. The list of seed nodes includes several hundred nodes, identified according to the standard established by BIP-0155. Thus, seed nodes are the third method a Bitcoin node uses to connect to the network, after the possible use of the `peers.dat` file, created by the node itself, and querying the DNS seeds.

*Note that seed nodes must not be confused with “DNS seeds”, which are the second way of establishing connections.*

entries.title: SEEDKEEPER
entries.body: Smart card developed by Satochip to securely back up mnemonic phrases and passwords. Secrets are stored in an EAL6+ certified secure element, protected by a PIN code. The SeedKeeper can hold at least 50 distinct secrets and allows duplication to a second card to create a backup.

entries.title: SEEDQR
entries.body:
Format for representing a recovery phrase as a QR code. Developed by the SeedSigner project, SeedQR encodes each word of the BIP-0039 mnemonic phrase by its index in the word list (four-digit position, padded with zeros), then concatenates these indices into a single numeric string. The numeric mode of QR codes makes it possible to obtain a compact result.

A variant called Compact SeedQR directly encodes the binary entropy of the phrase (128 bits for 12 words, 256 bits for 24 words), which reduces the size of the QR code by 35 to 40%. The format is adopted by several signing devices such as SeedSigner, Coldcard Q and Blockstream Jade.

SeedQR offers an alternative to the classic transcription in words: the phrase can be backed up on a physical medium (metal, paper) in the form of a QR code, then scanned directly by the signing device to import the *seed* without manual entry.

entries.title: SEEDSIGNER
entries.body:
*Open source* DIY (do-it-yourself) hardware wallet project based on a Raspberry Pi Zero, a screen and a camera. SeedSigner is designed to generate and handle Bitcoin private keys in an *air-gapped* manner and communicates exclusively via QR codes.

Its main characteristic is its “*stateless*” nature: the device keeps no data in memory between uses, which means that the mnemonic phrase must be entered each time it is used, by scanning a QR code. This approach eliminates the risk of keys being extracted from the device in the event of physical access.

The software is entirely *open source* and the cost of building it is fairly low, which makes it an accessible solution for signing transactions or managing a multisig. Since it can be assembled from general-purpose computer hardware, it is also an accessible solution for people living under an authoritarian regime.

entries.title: SEEDXOR
entries.body:
Method of splitting a Bitcoin recovery phrase into several parts using the XOR operation, introduced by Coinkite for Coldcard hardware wallets. The principle consists of dividing a mnemonic phrase of 12 or 24 words into two or more fragments that are themselves valid BIP-0039 phrases. To reconstruct the original phrase, all the parts must be recombined by XOR (an N-of-N scheme, not M-of-N).

Since each fragment is a functional mnemonic phrase, it can serve as a decoy wallet loaded with a small amount, thus offering a form of plausible deniability: an attacker cannot distinguish a SeedXOR fragment from an ordinary recovery phrase. The calculation can be done manually using printable worksheets, or directly on a Coldcard.

entries.title: SEGWIT
entries.body:
SegWit, an acronym for “*Segregated Witness*” (Separate Witness), is an update to the Bitcoin protocol introduced in August 2017. It aims to solve several technical problems, including the question of the network's transaction capacity, the problem of transaction malleability, and making future protocol modifications easier.

This soft fork modifies the structure of transactions by moving the signature data to a separate structure. Concretely, with SegWit, signatures are removed from the traditional transaction structure and inserted into a distinct data structure committed in a separate Merkle tree within the block; these are the witnesses (*witness*). This separation makes it possible to increase the effective capacity of each block by replacing the old 1 MB limit with a new limit of 4 million weight units (4 MWU), while remaining backward compatible with old nodes. This modification also solves the problem of transaction malleability. Before SegWit, signatures could be modified before a transaction was confirmed, which changed the transaction identifier. This made it difficult to build complex transactions, because an unconfirmed transaction could see its identifier change. By separating the signatures, SegWit makes transactions non-malleable, because any change in the signatures no longer affects the transaction identifier (TXID), but only the witness identifier (WTXID). By solving the malleability problem, SegWit paved the way for other developments layered on top of the Bitcoin system, notably the Lightning Network, which enables fast, low-cost transactions.

entries.title: SEGWIT V0
entries.body: Post-SegWit script version 0. SegWit V0 scripts represent the first family of scripts introduced with the SegWit update of 2017. P2WPKH and P2WSH scripts embody the SegWit V0 version. The corresponding addresses always begin with `bc1q` and are encoded in `Bech32` format.

entries.title: SEGWIT V1
entries.body: Post-SegWit script version 1. SegWit V1 scripts represent the second family of scripts introduced after the SegWit update of 2017. Specifically, SegWit V1 scripts were introduced with the Taproot update in 2021. The P2TR script is of the SegWit V1 version. The corresponding addresses always begin with `bc1p` and are encoded in `Bech32m` format.

entries.title: SEGWIT2X
entries.body:
Controversial hard fork attempt aimed at doubling the block size limit on Bitcoin, while integrating SegWit. SegWit2x was introduced at the New York Agreement in 2017, a confidential meeting of more than 50 companies from the ecosystem that aimed to find a solution for scaling the system. SegWit2x sought to increase Bitcoin's transaction capacity by raising the maximum size of a block to 2 MB, compared with the original 1 MB. The hard fork was scheduled for block 494,784, that is, during the month of November 2017.

Despite the activation of SegWit in August 2017, the 2X project to double the size failed to obtain a consensus, notably because of the “NO2X” opposition campaign, which led to its cancellation at the beginning of November. This episode was perceived by many users and developers as an attack on Bitcoin, as part of the Blocksize War.

*SegWit2x is sometimes also called “B2X” or “S2X”. Initially, its name was “SegWit2Mb”.*

entries.title: SEIGNIORAGE
entries.body:
Revenue that a currency issuer derives from the difference between the face value of the money produced and its cost of production. Historically, seigniorage referred to the profit made by the lord or sovereign when minting metal coins: the cost of the metal and of the minting was lower than the nominal value of the coin put into circulation.

In the modern fiat monetary system, seigniorage takes on considerable scale. Central banks create money at almost zero cost (by a simple accounting entry or by printing), while this money circulates at its nominal value. This mechanism constitutes a form of implicit taxation on holders of existing money, whose purchasing power is diluted by each new issuance.

In Bitcoin, there is no seigniorage in the traditional sense. The issuance of new bitcoins through the block subsidy does not benefit a central authority, but pays miners in return for a real cost: the energy and hardware needed for mining. Eventually, the block subsidy will be zero.

entries.title: SELF-CUSTODY
entries.body: Refers to the practice whereby a user keeps direct control of their private keys, and therefore of their bitcoins, without depending on an external entity to manage their assets.

entries.title: SELFISH MINING
entries.body:
Strategy (or attack) in mining, where a miner or a group of miners intentionally withholds blocks with valid proof of work without immediately broadcasting them to the network. The goal is to keep a lead over the other miners in terms of proof of work, which potentially allows them to mine several blocks in a row and publish them all at once, thus maximizing their gains. In other words, the group of attacking miners does not mine on the last block validated by the whole network, but rather on a block they created themselves, which differs from the one validated by the network.

This process generates a kind of secret branch of the blockchain, which remains unknown to the whole network until this alternative chain potentially surpasses the honest blockchain. Once the attacking miners' secret chain becomes longer (that is, it contains more accumulated work) than the honest, public chain, it is then broadcast across the whole network. At that moment, the network's nodes, which follow the chain with the most accumulated work, will synchronize on this new chain. There is therefore a reorganization.

*Selfish mining* is annoying for users, because it reduces the security of the system by wasting part of the network's computing power. If successful, it also leads to blockchain reorganizations, thus affecting the reliability of transaction confirmations for users. This practice nonetheless remains risky for the group of attacking miners, because it is often more profitable to mine normally on top of the last publicly known block rather than allocate computing power to a secret branch that will probably never surpass the honest blockchain. The greater the number of blocks in the reorganization, the lower the probability that the attack succeeds.

*Note that a selfish mining attack must not be confused with a block withholding attack.*

entries.title: SENTINEL
entries.body: *Watch-only* wallet Android application, originally developed by the Samourai Wallet team and now maintained by the community. Sentinel makes it possible to monitor the balances and transaction history of a Bitcoin wallet by importing its extended public keys (`xpub`, `ypub`, `zpub`), without ever exposing the private keys. The application supports PSBTs, connection via Tor and attachment to a personal Dojo node.

entries.title: SEQUENCER
entries.body: Specialized node responsible for ordering transactions and producing blocks in a rollup. The sequencer continuously monitors the mempool, selects pending transactions (prioritized by fees), executes them against the rollup's current state and produces a new block at regular intervals. It then issues a signed “soft confirmation” (*soft confirmation*), providing a fast pre-confirmation to the network's full nodes. Periodically, the sequencer publishes commitments (*commitments*) to the base layer (Bitcoin, in the case of Citrea) to permanently anchor the order of the blocks. The sequencer can influence the order of transactions and cause availability delays (*liveness*), but cannot falsify the rollup's state or steal funds, because validity proofs and the on-chain availability of data guarantee the integrity of state transitions. Decentralization of the sequencer is an active research topic in the rollup ecosystem.

entries.title: SETTINGS.JSON
entries.body: File used in Bitcoin Core to store dynamic settings defined via the graphical interface (GUI) or via RPCs. It keeps information about the user's configurations, such as the wallets that are open, for example. When Bitcoin Core is restarted, this file makes it possible to automatically reopen the wallets that were active before the application was closed. If a wallet is closed via the GUI, it is also removed from this file, and it will therefore not be automatically reopened at the next startup.

entries.title: SHA256
entries.body: Acronym for “*Secure Hash Algorithm 256 bits*”. It is a cryptographic hash function producing a 256-bit digest. Designed by the *National Security Agency* (NSA) in the early 2000s, it became a federal standard for processing sensitive data. In the Bitcoin protocol, the `SHA256` function is ubiquitous. It is used to hash block headers as part of proof of work. `SHA256` is also used in the process of deriving a receiving address from a public key. It is also used to aggregate transactions and witnesses within Merkle trees in blocks. `SHA256` is also found in key fingerprint calculation, in the calculation of certain checksums and in many other processes around Bitcoin. When it is applied twice in a row, it is called a `HASH256`. This double application is the one mostly used on Bitcoin. When `SHA256` is used together with the `RIPEMD160` function, it is called a `HASH160`. This double hash is used for key fingerprints and for hashing public keys. The `SHA256` function belongs to the SHA 2 family.

entries.title: SHA512
entries.body: Acronym for “*Secure Hash Algorithm 512 bits*”. It is a cryptographic hash function producing a 512-bit digest. It was designed by the *National Security Agency* (NSA) in the early 2000s. For Bitcoin, the `SHA512` function is not used directly within the protocol, but it is used in child key derivations at the application level, according to BIP-0032 and BIP-0039. In these processes, it is used several times in the `HMAC` algorithm, as well as in the `PBKDF2` key derivation function. The `SHA512` function belongs to the SHA 2 family, like `SHA256`. Its operation is, moreover, very similar to the latter.

entries.title: SHAMIR SECRET SHARING - SSS
entries.body:
Cryptographic secret sharing scheme designed by Adi Shamir in 1979. It makes it possible to divide a secret into n distinct shares, such that a minimum of t shares is needed to reconstruct the original secret, while t-1 shares or fewer reveal no information about it. The (t, n) parameters are defined when the shares are created.

In the Bitcoin ecosystem, Shamir's secret sharing is used in several contexts. The Codex32 protocol, formalized in BIP-0093, relies on this scheme to allow the backup and manual reconstruction of seeds. It is also an option offered on Trezor *hardware wallets*. Threshold signature protocols such as FROST also rely on this mechanism during the distributed key generation phase.

entries.title: SHARDS - LIGHTNING
entries.body:
In the context of *Multi-Path Payments (MPP)* or *Atomic Multi-Path Payments (AMP)*, a shard is a fraction of an overall payment. Each shard represents a part of the total payment that is routed separately along a different route on Lightning.

In MPP, all the shards share the same secret, whereas in AMP, each shard has a unique partial secret. The recipient gathers the shards to reconstitute and finalize the complete payment. This mechanism makes it possible to work around liquidity limitations on a single channel.

entries.title: SHARDS - RGB
entries.body: In the RGB protocol, a *Shard* represents a distinct branch within the directed acyclic graph (DAG) that traces the history of a contract's *State Transitions*. It constitutes a coherent subset of the set of transitions, corresponding for example to the sequence of operations needed to attest to the validity of a particular asset since the *Genesis*. This mechanism makes it possible to isolate specific segments of the overall history, in order to facilitate client-side validation.

entries.title: SHAREDCOIN
entries.body: Bitcoin coin mixing service launched in 2013 by Blockchain.info, but no longer in operation today. This service offered users the ability to improve their privacy on Bitcoin by combining their transactions with those of other people, using a mixing technique similar to coinjoins. SharedCoin provided a form of privacy without requiring trust in the coordinator, because users' coins remained under their control throughout the process. Unlike the centralized mixing services of the time, the bitcoins could not be stolen by the intermediary. SharedCoin subsequently faced problems leading to the deanonymization of some of its mixes in early summer 2014.

entries.title: SHARES
entries.body:
In the context of mining pools, a share is an indicator used to quantify the contribution of an individual miner within the pool. This measure serves as the basis for calculating the reward that the pool redistributes to each miner. Each share corresponds to a hash that satisfies a difficulty target lower than that of the Bitcoin network.

To explain with an analogy, consider a 20-sided die. On Bitcoin, suppose that proof of work requires rolling below 3 to validate a block (that is, getting a result of 1 or 2). Now, imagine that within a mining pool, the difficulty target for a share is set at 10. Thus, for an individual miner in the pool, each die roll that gives a result below 10 counts as a valid share. These shares are then submitted to the pool by the miner, in order to claim their payment, even if they do not correspond to a valid result for a block on Bitcoin.

For each hash computed, an individual miner in a pool can encounter three different scenarios:
* If the hash value is greater than or equal to the difficulty target set by the pool for a share, then this hash is of no use. The miner then modifies their nonce to try a new hash: `hash > share > bloc`.
* If the hash is lower than the share's difficulty target, but greater than or equal to Bitcoin's difficulty target, then this hash constitutes a valid share that is nevertheless not sufficient to validate a block. The miner can send this hash to their pool to claim the reward associated with the share: `share > hash > bloc`.
* If the hash is lower than the Bitcoin network's difficulty target, it is considered both a valid share and a valid block. The miner submits this hash to their pool, which hurries to broadcast it on the Bitcoin network. This hash is also counted as a valid share for the miner: `share > bloc > hash`.

![Three zones of the hash: above the share target nothing is valid, below it a share, below the block target a block.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LoicPandul/Dictionnaire-de-Bitcoin/bab568e32351cc9f1240f49f5feedc242123d101/definitions/fr/s/shares/assets/image-1.png)

This share system is used to estimate the work done by each individual miner within a pool, without having to individually recompute all the hashes generated by a miner, which would be completely inefficient for the pool.

Mining pools adjust share difficulty to balance the verification load and to ensure that each miner, whether small or large, submits shares approximately every few seconds. This makes it possible to accurately calculate each miner's hashrate and to distribute rewards according to the chosen payout calculation method (PPS, PPLNS, TIDES...).

entries.title: SHARES DIFFICULTY
entries.body: Difficulty target higher than Bitcoin's (thus less difficult), defined by a mining pool to qualify a hash as a share and to evaluate the contribution of each individual miner in the pool. To efficiently manage the verification load and ensure that each miner, regardless of their computing power, submits shares regularly, pools adjust share difficulty. The difficulty assigned to each miner determines the number of shares they accumulate: for example, if a miner has an assigned difficulty of 10 and submits 5 valid proofs of work at this difficulty, they obtain 50 shares. A more powerful miner with a difficulty of 100 who submits 7 valid proofs of work will receive 700 shares. This system makes it possible to precisely quantify each miner's hashrate and to distribute rewards according to the chosen payout calculation method (PPS, PPLNS, TIDES...).

entries.title: SHITCOIN
entries.body: Pejorative expression frequently used in the cryptocurrency world to describe altcoins deemed worthless or without a future. This term is used in two distinct contexts: in the general cryptocurrency community, it designates a project that lacks technological innovation, that presents no concrete use case, or that is mainly the product of excessive speculation. For maximalist bitcoiners, the term encompasses all cryptocurrencies other than bitcoin (BTC), making “shitcoin” a synonym for “altcoin”. The word is a combination of “shit” and “coin”. The initial use of the term goes back to a message posted by the user Ribuck on November 8, 2010 on the Bitcoin Talk forum.

entries.title: SHOR'S ALGORITHM
entries.body: Quantum algorithm invented in 1994 by Peter Shor that makes it possible to factor large integers into products of prime numbers in polynomial time. By reducing the number of operations needed to factor integers, Shor could make cryptographic algorithms based on this mathematical problem, such as RSA, impractical. Shor can be slightly modified to act on almost all algorithms that use a group structure. In particular, it already has an efficient variant for elliptic curve cryptography (ECDSA, Schnorr...). Shor and its close variants are therefore effective against asymmetric cryptography algorithms. At present, we do not yet have a quantum computer powerful and stable enough to successfully run Shor's algorithm.

entries.title: SIDECAR CHANNEL
entries.body:
Lightning channel opened by a third party (party A) for the benefit of another user (party B), toward a routing node (party C). This mechanism, introduced in Lightning Pool by Lightning Labs, makes it possible to onboard new users onto the Lightning Network without them needing to hold bitcoin beforehand to fund a channel.

Concretely, a node operator with a funded Pool account can buy a channel lease (*channel lease*) on behalf of a third party. The selling routing node then opens a channel directly to the beneficiary, who can immediately receive payments through a peer that is well connected to the network. This model creates a source of revenue for intermediary operators, while promoting the decentralization of the network since new users connect through a diversity of peers rather than a single point. *Sidecar channels* also make it possible to create dual-funded channels (*dual-funded*) and can be deployed as *turbo channels*, without waiting for on-chain confirmations.

entries.title: SIDECAR TICKET
entries.body: Token allowing the beneficiary of a *sidecar channel* purchased on Lightning Pool to claim the opening of the channel. When a participant in a Pool auction buys a channel for a third party (for example a mobile wallet), they generate a *sidecar ticket* containing the information needed for the opening. The beneficiary presents this ticket so that the seller opens the channel directly to them. This mechanism allows users who do not directly participate in Pool auctions to benefit from inbound liquidity.

entries.title: SIDECHAIN
entries.body:
Blockchain designed to operate in parallel with Bitcoin's main blockchain. The two chains are connected using a two-way peg, which ensures that the asset circulating on the sidechain keeps the same value as the bitcoin on the main chain. The sidechain has its own consensus mechanism, which can be independent or can rely in part on that of the main chain. It generally makes it possible to use features that are not available directly on the main chain, or to benefit from improved features, such as: more flexibility in development, faster and/or more private transactions, or higher transaction capacity. To do so, the sidechain makes trade-offs compared to the main chain.

The concept of a sidechain was initially presented in 2014 by Adam Back, Matt Corallo, Luke Dashjr, Mark Friedenbach, Gregory Maxwell, Andrew Miller, Andrew Poelstra, Jorge Timón and Pieter Wuille. Currently, the best-known sidechains on Bitcoin are Liquid and RSK (Rootstock). However, these remain very little used compared to other layer-two solutions with a different model, such as the Lightning Network.

entries.title: SIGHASH FLAG
SIGHASH_ALL
entries.body: Type of SigHash Flag used in Bitcoin transaction signatures to indicate that the signature applies to all components of the transaction. By using `SIGHASH_ALL`, the signer covers all inputs and all outputs. This means that neither the inputs nor the outputs can be modified after signing without invalidating the signature. This type of SigHash Flag is the most common in Bitcoin transactions, because it ensures complete finality and integrity of the transaction.

entries.title: SIGHASH_ALL | SIGHASH_ACP
entries.body: Type of SigHash Flag (`0x81`) combined with the modifier `SIGHASH_ANYONECANPAY` (`SIGHASH_ACP`) used in Bitcoin transaction signatures. This combination specifies that the signature applies to all outputs and only to one specific input of the transaction. `SIGHASH_ALL | SIGHASH_ANYONECANPAY` allows other participants to add additional inputs to the transaction after its initial signature. It is particularly useful in collaborative scenarios, such as crowdfunding transactions, where different contributors can add their own inputs while preserving the integrity of the outputs committed to by the initial signer.

entries.title: SIGHASH_ANYPREVOUT
entries.body:
Proposal to implement a new modifier SigHash Flag in Bitcoin, introduced with BIP-0118. `SIGHASH_ANYPREVOUT` allows greater flexibility in transaction management, particularly for advanced applications such as payment channels on the Lightning Network and the Eltoo update. The `SIGHASH_ANYPREVOUT` makes it possible to bind the signature to no specific prior UTXO (*Any Previous Output*). Used in combination with `SIGHASH_ALL`, it would allow signing all inputs and all outputs of a transaction, but without committing to the specific UTXO spent by each input. This would allow the signature to be reused for different transactions, as long as certain specified conditions are met.

*This modifier SigHash `SIGHASH_ANYPREVOUT` is inherited from the idea of `SIGHASH_NOINPUT` initially proposed by Joseph Poon in 2016 to improve his idea of the Lightning Network.*

entries.title: SIGHASH_ANYPREVOUTANYSCRIPT
entries.body: Variant of the modifier SigHash Flag `SIGHASH_ANYPREVOUT` in Bitcoin, introduced in BIP-0118. This SigHash works like `SIGHASH_ANYPREVOUT`, but in addition to not committing to the specific UTXO spent, the signature commits neither to the script (scriptCode/tapscript) nor to the amount of the input. This allows the same signature to be reused to spend any UTXO using the same BIP-0118 public key, regardless of the associated script or amount.

entries.title: SIGHASH_NONE - 0X02
entries.body: Type of SigHash Flag used in Bitcoin transaction signatures to indicate that the signature applies to all of the transaction's inputs, but to none of its outputs. The use of `SIGHASH_NONE` implies that the signer commits only to the inputs, but allows the outputs to remain undetermined or modifiable after signing. This type of signature is useful in cases where the signer wishes to authorize other parties to decide how the bitcoins will be distributed in this transaction.

entries.title: SIGHASH_NONE | SIGHASH_ACP
entries.body: Type of SigHash Flag (`0x82`) combined with the modifier `SIGHASH_ANYONECANPAY` (`SIGHASH_ACP`) used in Bitcoin transaction signatures. This combination indicates that the signature applies only to one specific input, without committing to any output. This allows other participants to freely add additional inputs and to modify all of the transaction's outputs.

entries.title: SIGHASH_SINGLE - 0X03
entries.body: Type of SigHash Flag used in Bitcoin transaction signatures to indicate that the signature applies to all the inputs of the transaction and to a single output, corresponding to the index of the same signed input. Thus, each input signed with `SIGHASH_SINGLE` is specifically linked to a particular output. The other outputs are not committed to by the signature and can therefore be modified later. This type of signature is useful in complex transactions, where participants want to link certain inputs to specific outputs, while leaving flexibility for the other outputs of the transaction.

entries.title: SIGHASH_SINGLE | SIGHASH_ACP
entries.body: Type of SigHash Flag (`0x83`) combined with the `SIGHASH_ANYONECANPAY` modifier (`SIGHASH_ACP`) used in Bitcoin transaction signatures. This combination specifies that the signature applies to a single specific input and only to the output with the same index as that input. The other inputs and outputs can be added or modified by other parties. This configuration is useful for collaborative transactions where participants can add their own inputs to fund a specific output.

entries.title: SIGN-TO-CONTRACT
entries.body:
Cryptographic protocol that makes it possible to commit arbitrary data into the nonce of a digital signature, without this commitment being visible from the outside. This technique is the analogue of Pay-to-Contract, but applied to the nonce (the random value `k`) rather than to the public key. The principle relies on "tweaking" the nonce: from an original nonce `k` and a commitment `c`, a new nonce `k' = k + H(R \| c)` is computed, where `R = k \cdot G` is the public point of the original nonce and `H` a hash function. The resulting public nonce `R' = k' \cdot G` appears as an arbitrary point on the curve, but it encodes a verifiable commitment to `c`. To prove the commitment, it is enough to reveal `R` and `c`.

This construction has several applications in Bitcoin. In particular, it makes it possible to timestamp documents: the fingerprint of a file is inserted into the nonce of an ordinary transaction. It is also the underlying mechanism of the anti-exfiltration protocol (anti-exfil), where a host software injects its own entropy into the nonce of a *hardware wallet* to prevent the leakage of the private key through a covert channel.

entries.title: SIGNALING
entries.body:
Mechanism by which miners indicate their support for or readiness for a soft fork proposal on Bitcoin. Signaling is done by setting a specific bit in the `nVersion` field of the header of the blocks they mine, in accordance with the process defined by BIP-0009 (and its successors such as BIP-0008).

Each bit of the version field can be associated with a distinct soft fork proposal. When a miner sets the corresponding bit, they signal that they have updated their software and are ready to enforce the new rules.

entries.title: SIGNET
entries.body: Specific versions of the Bitcoin network designed for development and testing. Signets simulate the behavior of the main network (*mainnet*) but with the ability to control various parameters. They thus provide an environment to test new features or modifications without risking disrupting the main network and without incurring its fees. Compared to *testnet*, signets offer more structured control over block generation, often managed by one or more trusted entities or by a custom consensus mechanism. This makes it possible to create more predictable test scenarios, compared to *testnet*, which is subject to the vagaries of mining, in the same way as *mainnet*.

entries.title: SIGOPS
SILENT PAYMENTS
entries.body:
Method for using static Bitcoin addresses to receive payments without producing address reuse, without interaction and without any visible on-chain link between the different payments and the static address. This technique eliminates the need to generate new fresh receiving addresses for each transaction, which avoids the usual interactions in Bitcoin where the recipient must provide a new address to the payer.

With Silent Payments, the payer uses the recipient's public keys (spend public key and scan public key) and the sum of the private keys of their own inputs to generate a fresh address for each payment. Only the recipient, thanks to their private keys, can compute the private key corresponding to this payment address. ECDH (*Elliptic-Curve Diffie-Hellman*), a cryptographic key exchange algorithm, is used to establish a shared secret which is then used to derive the receiving address and the private key (only on the recipient's side). To identify the Silent Payments intended for them, recipients must scan the blockchain and examine each transaction matching the protocol's criteria. Unlike BIP-0047, which uses a notification transaction to establish the payment channel, Silent Payments remove this step, which saves one transaction. However, the trade-off is that the recipient must scan all the potential transactions to determine, by applying ECDH, whether they are addressed to them.

For example, Bob's static address `B` represents the concatenation of his scan public key and his spend public key:
```math
B\ =\ B_{scan}\ \Vert\ B_{spend}
```
These keys are simply derived from the following path:

```text
scan : m / 352' / 0' / 0' / 1' / 0
spend : m / 352' / 0' / 0' / 0' / 0
```

This static address is published by Bob. Alice retrieves it to make a Silent Payment to Bob. She computes the payment address `P_0` belonging to Bob in this way:
```math
P_0\ =\ B_{spend}\ +\ hash(inputHash \cdot a \cdot B_{scan}\ \Vert\ 0) \cdot G
```
Where:
```math
inputHash\ =\ hash(outpoint_L\ \Vert\ A)
```
With:
* `B_{scan}`: Bob's scan public key (static address);
* `B_{spend}`: Bob's spend public key (static address);
* `A`: The sum of the input public keys (tweak);
* `a`: The tweak private key, that is, the sum of all the key pairs used in the `scriptPubKey` of the UTXOs spent as inputs of Alice's transaction;
* `outpoint_L`: The smallest outpoint (lexicographically) used as an input of Alice's transaction;
* `\Vert`: The concatenation (an operation that consists of placing the operands end to end);
* `G`: The generator point of the elliptic curve `secp256k1`;
* `hash`: The SHA256 hash function tagged with `BIP0352/SharedSecret`;
* `P_0`: The first public key / unique address for the payment to Bob;
* `0`: An integer making it possible to generate several unique payment addresses.

Bob scans the blockchain to find his Silent Payment in this way:
```math
P_0\ =\ B_{spend}\ +\ hash(inputHash \cdot b_{scan} \cdot A\ \Vert\ 0) \cdot G
```
With:
* `b_{scan}`: Bob's scan private key.

If he finds `P_0` as an address that contains a Silent Payment addressed to him, he computes `p_0`, the private key making it possible to spend the funds sent by Alice to `P_0`:
```math
p_0\ =\ (b_{spend}\ +\ hash(inputHash \cdot b_{scan} \cdot A\ \Vert\ 0)) \mod n
```
With:
* `b_{spend}`: Bob's spend private key;
* `n`: the order of the elliptic curve `secp256k1`.

In addition to this basic version, it is also possible to use labels, which make it possible to generate several different static addresses from a single base static address, with the aim of separating several uses, without unreasonably multiplying the work required during scanning.

entries.title: SILK ROAD
entries.body:
Silk Road was a *dark web* platform founded by Ross Ulbricht, also known by the pseudonym *Dread Pirate Roberts*. Launched in 2011, this online marketplace allowed users to buy and sell products and services, both licit and illicit, while preserving their anonymity through the use of Tor and bitcoin payments. Silk Road offered a varied range of items, mainly drugs and normally prescription-only medicines, but excluded activities deemed contrary to natural-law principles, such as the sale of hitman services or child sexual abuse material.

The platform reflected Ross Ulbricht's agorist convictions, by promoting a free and unregulated market, thus escaping government control and taxation. Silk Road played a significant role in the initial adoption of Bitcoin in the early 2010s, by contributing to its notoriety and its use beyond *cypherpunk* circles.

Silk Road was shut down in 2013. Ross Ulbricht was arrested the same year and sentenced to two life sentences plus 40 years, without the possibility of parole, along with restitution of 183 million dollars. This sentence raises questions about the proportionality of the penalties imposed for non-violent online crimes. Ross Ulbricht was finally pardoned by President Donald Trump on January 21, 2025, after spending more than 11 years in prison.

entries.title: SIMPLICITY
entries.body: Low-level programming language designed by Russell O'Connor at Blockstream to express contracts on blockchains that rely on the UTXO model. Presented in a white paper in 2017, Simplicity differs from languages like Solidity (Ethereum) in that it is not Turing-complete: it can express any finite function, but prohibits unbounded loops and global state. This restriction makes it possible to guarantee that every execution terminates, and that the resource cost of a program is known before its execution. The language was deployed on Liquid in July 2025, where it gives asset issuers the ability to create verifiable contracts. Unlike Miniscript, which is limited to signatures, timelocks and hash preimages within Script, Simplicity can express arbitrary functions, but requires a consensus environment distinct from that of Bitcoin.

entries.title: SIMPLIFIED PAYMENT VERIFICATION
entries.body:
Method allowing light clients to verify Bitcoin transactions without downloading the entire blockchain. A node that uses SPV downloads only the block headers, which are much lighter than full blocks. When it needs to verify a transaction, the SPV node requests a Merkle proof from full nodes to confirm that the transaction is included in a specific block. This approach is efficient for devices with limited resources, such as smartphones, but implies a dependence on full nodes, which can reduce security and increase the trust required.

*The acronym "SPV" is often used to refer to this method.*

entries.title: SINGLE-SIG
entries.body: Bitcoin wallet configuration in which a single private key is enough to sign a transaction and authorize the spending of funds. This mode of operation, also called "single signature", is the simplest and most widespread form of securing a wallet. Unlike multisig, which requires several signatures coming from different keys to validate a transaction, single-sig relies only on the possession of a single seed.

entries.title: SINGLE-USE SEAL
entries.body: Refers to a promise of cryptographic commitment to a message that is still unknown, which will be revealed only once in the future and must be accessible to an entire determined audience. This mechanism aims to prevent the creation of multiple competing commitments for the same seal, which guarantees the uniqueness of each validation. By imposing this single-use constraint, the Single-use Seal is used on RGB to prevent double-spending.

entries.title: SLIP
entries.body: Acronym for "*SatoshiLabs Improvement Proposals*". It is a set of proposals aimed at improving or standardizing the use of Bitcoin, originating from SatoshiLabs, the company behind the Trezor hardware wallets. These proposals are often structured as extensions of BIPs (*Bitcoin Improvement Proposals*), with the aim of enriching existing standards. They set out technical decisions made by SatoshiLabs that do not find their place in the BIPs, but that remain relevant for other wallet software or hardware wallet developers, in particular to help standardize processes.

entries.title: SMALL BLOCKERS
entries.body: Name given to the supporters of keeping Bitcoin's block size at a low level during the Blocksize War between 2015 and 2017, in order to preserve the decentralization and security of the system. They support solutions like SegWit, believe that scaling should be done on upper layers such as the Lightning Network, and support the implementation of changes via soft forks rather than hard forks.

entries.title: SMPPS
entries.body: Acronym for "*Shared Maximum Pay Per Share*". It is a method for calculating miner remuneration in the context of mining pools. It is a variant of the PPS method. It limits payouts so that the pool never pays more than what it has earned in block rewards. Thus, even if miners submit valid shares, the total reward distributed cannot exceed the pool's revenue. This method aims to maintain the financial balance of the pool while using a pay-per-task payment system, which reduces the variance for individual miners.

entries.title: SMT - SPARSE MERKLE TREE
entries.body: A data structure that extends the properties of a classic Merkle tree by making it possible to produce proofs of non-inclusion in addition to proofs of inclusion. In an SMT, each element is placed at a position in the tree determined by the SHA-256 hash of its data: each bit of the hash indicates a left or right path through the binary tree. Because the majority of leaves remain empty, the tree is said to be "sparse" (*sparse*), which allows efficient generation and updating thanks to the pruning of empty branches. SMTs are used in the Taproot Assets protocol to manage asset transfers and to prove that a given asset has not been spent twice.

entries.title: SNAPSHOT
entries.body:
An instantaneous capture of the state of Bitcoin's UTXO set at a given block. A snapshot records all the UTXOs existing at that block height, forming a complete picture of all the unspent coins on the network.

The main use of the snapshot in Bitcoin is through the Assume UTXO mechanism, built into the Bitcoin Core client. When a new node is initialized, it can load a snapshot of the UTXO set that has been pre-computed and whose cryptographic fingerprint is verified. This approach allows the node to be functional almost immediately, without having to validate the entire blockchain history from the genesis block. Full verification of the chain is then carried out in the background.

entries.title: SNARK
entries.body: A cryptographic proof system whose acronym stands for *Succinct Non-interactive ARgument of Knowledge*. A SNARK allows a prover to convince a verifier that a statement is true, without interaction and without revealing the underlying data, by producing a very small proof (a few hundred bytes) that can be verified in constant time. This succinctness is the main advantage of SNARKs over STARKs. On the other hand, most SNARK constructions, such as Groth16, require a trusted setup ceremony (*trusted setup*) specific to the circuit being proven. If the secret parameters of this ceremony are compromised, it becomes possible to forge false proofs. SNARKs rely on hardness assumptions related to elliptic curves and are therefore not inherently resistant to quantum attacks. In the Bitcoin ecosystem, SNARKs are used notably to compress larger STARK proofs before their on-chain publication, as in the case of the Citrea rollup.

entries.title: SO - SPARK OPERATOR
entries.body:
An individual node within the *Spark Entity* (SE), participating in the threshold signing protocol that secures *off-chain* transfers in Spark. Each SO holds a fragment of the SE's key share, without ever possessing the complete key on its own. The set of SOs (or a threshold of them) cooperate via the FROST protocol to co-sign transactions and to refresh key shares during ownership transfers.

SOs also play a *watchtower* role: they monitor the Bitcoin blockchain to detect any fraudulent exit attempts by former owners.

If an SO is unavailable, transfers may be temporarily blocked, but users retain the ability to exit unilaterally to the main layer. At the launch of Spark, two operators (Lightspark and Flashnet) make up the SE, with the aim of widening the number of operators across various jurisdictions in order to spread the risk.

entries.title: SOFT FORK
entries.body: A modification of the protocol rules in a backward-compatible way. Unlike a hard fork, a soft fork does not result in the Bitcoin node network splitting into two distinct groups, provided that a majority of the computing power is on the updated chain. If all goes well, nodes with the update and nodes without the update therefore remain on the same blockchain. A modification is backward-compatible when it adds certain protocol rules or makes them more restrictive.

entries.title: SOLO MINING
entries.body:
A mining practice in which a miner uses their own equipment to search for valid proofs of work autonomously, without joining a mining pool. The solo miner operates their own full node to retrieve pending transactions, build their candidate blocks and attempt to find a hash satisfying the network's difficulty target.

In *solo mining*, the miner keeps the entire block reward when they manage to find a valid block, with no pool fees to pay, and retains full control over the selection of transactions included in their blocks. On the other hand, the probability of finding a block is directly proportional to the miner's hashrate relative to the total hashrate of the network. For an individual miner with a modest hashrate, this probability is extremely low, which makes income very irregular and unpredictable. It is this high variance that motivated the emergence of mining pools, where miners pool their computing power to obtain more frequent and regular payouts.

entries.title: SOROBAN
entries.body: An encrypted communication protocol established on Tor that allows collaboration with other users in the context of a Cahoots transaction. Soroban was developed by the Samourai Wallet teams to facilitate the exchange of partially signed transactions (PSBT) between users who wish to carry out collaborative transactions (*Stowaway*, *Stonewall x2*...). This protocol is used in the Samourai Wallet application and in the Sparrow Wallet software.

entries.title: SOURCEFORGE
entries.body: A web platform for hosting and distributing *open source* software, founded in 1999. SourceForge played a historic role in the early days of Bitcoin: the project was registered there by Satoshi Nakamoto in November 2008, and the first version of the software (v0.1) was published there in January 2009. The platform also hosted the Bitcoin community's initial discussion forum, as well as the bitcoin-dev mailing list in its early days. The Bitcoin project later migrated to GitHub, which became the main collaboration tool for protocol development.

entries.title: SPARK
entries.body:
An open source upper-layer protocol built on Bitcoin, developed by Lightspark, designed to enable instant, very low-cost transactions while preserving users' self-custody. Spark relies mainly on statechain technology: rather than moving bitcoins on-chain with each transfer, the protocol modifies the spending authorization shared between the user and a group of operators called the *Spark Entity* (SE). The SE is composed of several *Spark Operators* (SO) who jointly take part in a shared signing protocol. It is enough for a single operator to be honest to prevent any collusion with a former owner.

Unlike the Lightning Network, which requires the management of payment channels, Spark transfers UTXO ownership off-chain without liquidity constraints or channel management. The protocol is natively compatible with Lightning: users can send and receive Lightning payments without operating a node. Spark also supports the issuance of tokens (BTKN) and stablecoins directly on Bitcoin. The user retains at all times the ability to withdraw their funds to the main layer unilaterally, without permission from the SE. Transfers between Spark wallets settle in under a second, with no fees.

entries.title: SPARK SERVICE PROVIDER
entries.body:
A service provider within the Spark ecosystem, whose main role is to facilitate deposits and withdrawals between Bitcoin's main layer and Spark. Several SSPs can coexist within the same Spark network.

SSPs also ensure interoperability with the Lightning Network by acting as intermediaries for Lightning payments. When a Spark user wishes to pay a Lightning invoice, the SSP executes an *atomic swap*.

entries.title: SPARK TREE
entries.body:
An offchain tree structure used in the Spark protocol to expand a single UTXO into several sub-units of value, in order to solve the problem of classic statechains, which required the transfer of an entire UTXO. The tree is made up of branches (*branch transactions*) and leaves (*leaf transactions*).

The root of the tree corresponds to the on-chain UTXO (`Txn0`), whose operator key is permanently destroyed. The branches are intermediate transactions maintained off-chain, without a timelock, which can only be spent through the aggregation of the keys of all the leaves located beneath them. The leaves are the terminal transactions held by individual users, each associated with an exit transaction with a relative timelock.

The splitting of a leaf relies on a key additivity property: the parent key is split into several child keys whose sum equals the original key (`a_0 = a_1 + a_2 + \ldots + a_n`). This property also allows leaves to be re-aggregated.

entries.title: SPARKSCAN
entries.body: A public explorer and analytics suite dedicated to the Spark protocol. Sparkscan makes it possible to look up addresses, transactions, tokens (BTKN) and real-time activity on the Spark network.

entries.title: SPARROW WALLET
entries.body: A Bitcoin wallet software for desktop computers (Windows, macOS, Linux), designed for users who want complete control over their Bitcoin transactions. Sparrow supports most of the *hardware wallets* on the market via PSBT, multisig, *coin control*, *labelling*... It allows connection to one's own Bitcoin node (Bitcoin Core or Electrum server) for sovereign verification of transactions, but can also work with a public server. The software is open source.

entries.title: SPECTER
entries.body: An open source software suite dedicated to managing Bitcoin wallets, with a particular emphasis on multisig configurations.
