Specter Desktop is a desktop application that interfaces directly with a personal Bitcoin Core node to create and manage singlesig and multisig wallets, compatible with most of the *hardware wallets* on the market (Trezor, Ledger, Coldcard, etc.). The project also includes Specter DIY, an open source *firmware* that makes it possible to build one's own *signing device* from standard electronic components.

entries.title: SPEEDY TRIAL
entries.body:
A soft fork activation method initially conceptualized for Taproot in early 2021 by David A. Harding, based on an idea by Russell O'Connor. Its principle is to use the BIP-0008 method with a `LOT` parameter set to `faux`, while reducing the activation period to only 3 months. This reduction of the voting period allows a quick verification of miner approval. If the required approval threshold is reached during one of the periods, the soft fork is then locked in. It will be activated several months later, thus giving miners the time needed to update their software.

The success of this method for Taproot, which benefited from broad consensus within the Bitcoin community, does not however guarantee its effectiveness for all upgrades. Although the Speedy Trial method allows faster activation, some developers express concerns about its future use. They fear that it could lead to too rapid a succession of soft forks, which could potentially threaten the stability and security of the Bitcoin protocol. Compared to BIP-0008 with the `LOT=true` parameter, the Speedy Trial method is much less threatening for miners. No UASF is automatically planned. This activation method has not yet been formalized in a BIP.

*"Speedy Trial" is borrowed from a legal terminology that indicates an "expedited trial". This evokes the fact that the improvement proposal is quickly sent before the miners' court, so that we are made aware of their intentions. It is generally accepted to use the English term directly in French.*

entries.title: SPHINX
entries.body: A cryptographic packet format used by the Lightning Network to route payments privately via onion routing. Originally designed by George Danezis and Ian Goldberg in 2009 for mix networks, it encapsulates routing instructions in successive layers of encryption. Each intermediate node can only decrypt the layer intended for it, revealing only the next hop without knowing the sender or the final recipient.

entries.title: SPIDERPOOL
entries.body: A Bitcoin mining pool founded in China. SpiderPool is among the main mining pools in the world in terms of hashrate. It offers FPPS and PPLNS payout methods, and caters to both individual miners and professional mining farms.

entries.title: SPIRAL
entries.body:
A subsidiary of Block Inc. (formerly Square) dedicated to funding and developing *open source* Bitcoin projects. Created in 2019 under the name "Square Crypto", then renamed "Spiral" in 2021, the organization funds independent developers, designers and contributors working on Bitcoin and its ecosystem.

Spiral has notably supported projects such as Bitcoin Core or BTCPay Server. The organization also develops the Lightning Dev Kit (LDK) and the Bitcoin Dev Kit (BDK), two *open source* libraries that facilitate the integration of Bitcoin and Lightning into third-party applications.

entries.title: SPLICING
entries.body:
A Lightning Network mechanism that allows a payment channel to be resized without closing it, either by adding funds to it (*splice-in*) or by withdrawing funds to an on-chain output (*splice-out*). The channel remains fully operational throughout the operation.

Splicing creates a new 2-of-2 multisignature transaction that spends the existing funding UTXO into a new UTXO with the adjusted capacity. The channel first enters "*quiescence*" mode (STFU) to freeze its state, then the two parties negotiate the transaction via the interactive-tx protocol, where each can add inputs and outputs. Third parties can also join their own operations to this same transaction, which makes it possible to share the on-chain fees. During confirmation, the old and the new channel state coexist, which makes it possible to continue routing payments without interruption.

Splicing reduces from two to just one the number of on-chain transactions needed to adjust a channel's capacity. It also makes possible single-balance wallets that unify on-chain and Lightning funds into a single balance for the user.

entries.title: SPOF
entries.body: A single point of failure (SPOF, from the English "*Single Point of Failure*") refers, in computing, to a component or element of a system whose failure would cause the complete shutdown of, or a significant loss of functionality in, the whole system. It can be a piece of hardware, a piece of information, a piece of software, or a part of a network. For example, in the specific context of Bitcoin HD wallets, the 12- or 24-word recovery phrase is often a SPOF for the wallet. If its secrecy is not ensured, the entire wallet could be stolen. In the same way, its mere loss could result in the loss of all the bitcoins in the wallet.

entries.title: SPREAD - WST
entries.body:
In the Whirlpool Stat Tool software, the spread is an indicator for measuring the homogeneity of the mixing process from the point of view of a given coin. Two spreads are distinguished: the prospective one and the retrospective one.

The prospective spread is calculated as the ratio between the prospective anonset of your coin and the total number of coins created after your Tx0. For example, if there are 100 coins in your pool and your coin has an anonset of 70, the prospective spread of your coin is then 70%. 

The retrospective spread, for its part, is the ratio between the retrospective anonset of your coin and the total number of Tx0s created before the last mix of your coin. Thus, if the retrospective anonset of your coin is 95 and there were 100 Tx0s before your last mix, then the retrospective spread of your coin is 95%.

These two indicators make it possible to evaluate the effectiveness of your coin's mixing relative to the potential offered by the pool. A low prospective spread, such as 5% for example, indicates a large margin for possible improvement through additional mixes. Conversely, a high prospective spread, such as 97% for example, means that little additional anonset can be gained with additional coinjoins.

entries.title: SPY MINING
entries.body:
A practice in which a miner or a mining pool connects to a competing pool in order to receive the block header hash as soon as a new block is discovered by that pool. By obtaining this information before it is broadcast on the network, the spy miner can immediately start mining on the new block, without waiting for the network to receive and fully validate it.

This technique provides an advantage of a few seconds over miners who wait for the normal propagation of the block. *Spy mining* is a common practice in the mining industry, which contributes to a competitive environment where pools compete not only with the rest of the network, but also with each other. It is often associated with *validationless mining*, because the spy miner starts working on a new block without having verified all of its transactions.

entries.title: SRC-20
entries.body: A fungible token standard on Bitcoin that relies on the STAMPS protocol to inscribe metadata directly into UTXOs. Unlike the BRC-20 standard, which stores its data in the *witness* part of transactions (which can be pruned by nodes), SRC-20 data is inscribed in unspent outputs, which makes it permanent and non-deletable.

entries.title: STABLECOIN
entries.body: A category of cryptocurrency designed to maintain a stable value relative to a reference asset, often a fiat currency such as the US dollar.

entries.title: STACKER
entries.body: A term used in the Bitcoin community to describe the act of regularly accumulating sats. It is a long-term savings strategy that consists of buying bitcoin on a recurring basis, regardless of the market price, often through the DCA (*Dollar-Cost Averaging*) method.

entries.title: STALE SHARE
entries.body:
In the context of a mining pool, a stale share is a share (a portion of work) submitted by a miner after a new block has already been found, rendering the work done on the old block obsolete. This generally occurs because of network latency between the miner and the pool server: the miner keeps computing hashes on a block that is no longer current, because it has not yet received the notification of the new block.

Stale shares are rejected by the pool and are not counted in the calculation of the miner's payout. A stale share rate of around 1% is considered normal. A higher rate may indicate network connection problems, excessive latency between the miner and the pool server, or a very high hashrate that generates shares faster than the network can transmit them. To reduce the stale share rate, miners can prefer an Ethernet connection over Wi-Fi, choose a pool geographically close to their equipment, or use a mining proxy.

entries.title: STAMPS
entries.body: A protocol that makes it possible to embed formatted image data directly on the Bitcoin blockchain via raw multisignature transactions (P2MS). Stamps encodes the binary content of an image in base64 and adds it into the keys of a 1-of-3 P2MS. One key is real and is used to spend the funds, while the other two are fake keys (the associated private key is not known) that store the data. By encoding the data directly as public keys rather than using `OP_RETURN` outputs, images stored with the Stamps protocol are particularly intensive in terms of workload for nodes. This method notably creates multiple UTXOs, which increases the size of the UTXO set and poses problems for full nodes.

entries.title: STARK
entries.body: A cryptographic proof system whose acronym stands for *Scalable Transparent ARgument of Knowledge*. STARKs allow a prover to demonstrate the validity of a computation to a verifier, without revealing the underlying data and without requiring an initial trust setup (*trusted setup*). This "transparency" property distinguishes them from SNARKs, which generally require a prior setup ceremony. STARKs rely on hash functions and on the FRI protocol (*Fast Reed-Solomon Interactive Oracle Proof of Proximity*), which makes them resistant to quantum attacks. In return, STARK proofs are significantly larger than SNARK proofs (on the order of several tens of kilobytes), which makes them less suited to direct on-chain verification. To work around this limitation, it is common to wrap a STARK proof inside a more compact SNARK proof before publication. This is the approach adopted by the Citrea rollup on Bitcoin, via the RISC Zero framework.

entries.title: START9
entries.body:
An American company (Start9 Labs, Inc.) developing StartOS, a free operating system for personal servers. Like Umbrel, Start9 aims to democratize self-hosting by allowing non-technical users to install and manage *open source* applications on their own hardware, without depending on third-party *cloud* services.

Start9 sells preconfigured servers and offers a *marketplace* of self-hosted applications including Bitcoin Core, Lightning implementations, storage and communication solutions, etc.

entries.title: STASH
entries.body: In the context of the RGB protocol, the Stash refers to the set of data stored client-side by a user for one or more contracts. This data notably includes the history of transitions, the *consignments* as well as the validity proofs, which are indispensable to the client-side validation process (*Client-side Validation*). Each holder keeps only the relevant fragments of the history (*shards*) needed to verify and update their contracts.

entries.title: STATE EXTENSION
entries.body: In the context of the RGB protocol, a *State Extension* refers to a contractual operation that makes it possible to initiate an update of a contract's state through the redemption of previously declared *Valencies*. This procedure exploits a public right written into the contract to trigger a modification, which only becomes effective after being closed by a *State Transition*. The latter incorporates the definitive update of the contract's state.

entries.title: STATE TRANSITION
entries.body: In the context of the RGB protocol, the *State Transition* refers to the operation that makes it possible to evolve a contract's state toward a new configuration. It can modify both the data of the *Global State* and that of the *Owned States*. Each transition is strictly verified according to the rules defined in the contract's *Schema*, which guarantees that the modifications comply with the constraints established during the *Genesis*. This operation is anchored in the Bitcoin blockchain via a *commitment*.

entries.title: STATECHAIN
entries.body:
A higher-layer mechanism on Bitcoin that makes it possible to transfer ownership of a UTXO off-chain, without broadcasting an on-chain transaction. The concept was initially proposed by Ruben Somsen in 2018. It relies on a key share between the user and an entity (*Statechain Entity*). The UTXO remains locked on-chain in a multisignature address, but effective control changes hands through a renewal of the private key shares: when Alice transfers to Bob, the entity destroys its share associated with Alice and generates a new one with Bob. Alice's old share becomes unusable.

Security relies on the assumption that the entity actually deletes its old key shares. To reduce this trust risk, the entity can be distributed among several operators via a threshold signature protocol: it is enough for a single operator to be honest to guarantee the integrity of the transfer. A unilateral exit mechanism allows the user to recover their funds on-chain. Statechains are used notably by the Spark protocol for instant transfers of bitcoins and other tokens.

entries.title: STEALTH ADDRESS
entries.body: A privacy technique that allows a recipient to receive payments on single-use addresses, derived on the fly by the sender, without these addresses being publicly linkable to the recipient's identity. The principle relies on elliptic curve cryptography: the recipient publishes a static public key (the *stealth address*), and each sender generates an ephemeral receiving address by combining this public key with a shared secret derived by ECDH (*Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman*). Only the recipient, thanks to their private key, can identify and spend the funds received on these ephemeral addresses. This approach avoids address reuse. The *stealth address* concept was initially proposed by a BitcoinTalk forum user under the pseudonym "ByteCoin" in 2011, then formalized by Peter Todd in January 2014, and served as a foundation for the creation of the BIP-0047 and *Silent Payments* protocols.

entries.title: STEGANOGRAPHY
entries.body: Steganography is a technique consisting of concealing sensitive information within a seemingly innocuous cover object or medium (typically a signal such as text, sound, image, video, Bitcoin transaction, etc.), which will not arouse suspicion even if it is in plain sight; only a legitimate recipient will know that there is information there for them and where to look for it.

entries.title: STONEWALL
entries.body:
A specific form of Bitcoin transaction aimed at increasing users' privacy when spending by imitating a coinjoin between two people, without actually being one. Indeed, this transaction is not collaborative. A user can build it alone, involving only UTXOs belonging to them as inputs. You can therefore create a Stonewall transaction for any occasion, without needing to synchronize with another user.

The Stonewall transaction works as follows: as the transaction's input, the sender uses 2 UTXOs that belong to them. As output, the transaction produces 4 outputs, 2 of which will be of exactly the same amount. The other 2 will be change outputs. Among the 2 outputs of the same amount, only one will actually go to the payment recipient.

There are therefore only 2 roles in a Stonewall transaction:
* The sender, who makes the actual payment;
* The recipient, who may be unaware of the specific nature of the transaction and simply expects a payment from the sender.

![Stonewall: 2 inputs from the same sender and 4 outputs including two identical amounts imitate a coinjoin without a real collaborator.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LoicPandul/Dictionnaire-de-Bitcoin/bab568e32351cc9f1240f49f5feedc242123d101/definitions/fr/s/stonewall/assets/image-1.png)
Stonewall transactions are available on both the Samourai Wallet application and the Sparrow Wallet software.

The Stonewall structure adds a great deal of entropy to the transaction and muddies the trail for chain analysis. Seen from the outside, such a transaction can be interpreted as a small coinjoin between two people. But in reality, just like the Stonewall x2 transaction, it is a payment. This method therefore generates uncertainty in chain analysis, and even points toward false leads. Even if the outside observer manages to identify the pattern of the Stonewall transaction, they will not have all the information. They will not be able to determine which of the two UTXOs of the same amounts corresponds to the payment. Moreover, they will not be able to determine whether the two input UTXOs come from two different people or belong to a single person who merged them. This last point is due to the fact that Stonewall x2 transactions follow exactly the same pattern as Stonewall transactions. Seen from the outside and without additional information about the context, it is impossible to differentiate a Stonewall transaction from a Stonewall x2 transaction. Yet the former are not collaborative transactions, whereas the latter are. This adds even more doubt about this spend.

entries.title: STONEWALL X2
entries.body:
A specific form of Bitcoin transaction aimed at increasing users' privacy when spending, through collaboration with a third party not involved in that spend. This method simulates a mini-coinjoin between two participants, while making a payment to a third party. Stonewall x2 transactions are available on both the Samourai Wallet application and the Sparrow Wallet software (the two are interoperable).

Its operation is relatively simple: one uses a UTXO in one's possession to make the payment and asks for the help of a third person who also contributes a UTXO belonging to them. The transaction ends up with four outputs: two of them of equal amounts, one destined for the payment recipient's address, the other for an address belonging to the collaborator. A third UTXO is sent back to another address of the collaborator, allowing them to recover the initial amount (a neutral action for them, modulo mining fees), and a last UTXO returns to an address belonging to us, which constitutes the change of the payment. Three different roles are thus defined in Stonewall x2 transactions:
* The sender, who makes the actual payment;
* The collaborator, who makes bitcoins available in order to improve the transaction's anonymity set, while recovering their funds in full at the end;
* The recipient, who may be unaware of the specific nature of the transaction and simply expects a payment from the sender.

![Stonewall x2: 2 inputs from the sender and a collaborator, 4 outputs including two of identical amounts to blur the analysis.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LoicPandul/Dictionnaire-de-Bitcoin/bab568e32351cc9f1240f49f5feedc242123d101/definitions/fr/s/stonewall-x2/assets/image-1.png)

The Stonewall x2 structure adds a great deal of entropy to the transaction and muddies the trail for chain analysis. Seen from the outside, such a transaction can be interpreted as a small coinjoin between two people. But in reality, it is a payment. This method therefore generates uncertainty in chain analysis, and even points toward false leads. Even if the outside observer manages to identify the pattern of the Stonewall x2 transaction, they will not have all the information. They will not be able to determine which of the two UTXOs of the same amounts corresponds to the payment. Moreover, they will not be able to know who made the payment. Finally, they will not be able to determine whether the two input UTXOs come from two different people or belong to a single person who merged them. This last point is due to the fact that classic Stonewall transactions follow exactly the same pattern as Stonewall x2 transactions. Seen from the outside and without additional information about the context, it is impossible to differentiate a Stonewall transaction from a Stonewall x2 transaction. Yet the former are not collaborative transactions, whereas the latter are. This adds even more doubt about the spend.

entries.title: STRATUM
entries.body:
A network protocol layered on top of Bitcoin, specifically designed to optimize communication between individual miners and mining pool servers in order to increase their profitability. Stratum was announced in late 2012 by Marek Palatinus, better known by the pseudonym "Slush" and founder of the very first mining pool, Slush Pool, now renamed Braiins Pool. Stratum replaced the old Getwork protocol, which had become obsolete.

It is important to understand that Stratum is not built into Bitcoin as a rule, but is rather specific software used by pools. Although mining pools are free not to use it, Stratum has established itself as the reference for mining on Bitcoin for more than ten years. Its second version, Stratum V2, aims to improve Stratum and to reduce the centralization concerns associated with mining pools that the latter has given rise to.

entries.title: STRATUM V2
entries.body: An evolution of Stratum, the well-known network protocol layered on top of Bitcoin designed for mining. This type of protocol is designed to optimize communication between individual miners and mining pool servers in order to increase their profitability. Developed by the Braiins pool (formerly "Slush Pool"), Stratum V2 introduces several improvements, notably more efficient communication between miners and mining pools, thereby reducing the bandwidth required. It also reduces infrastructure needs for pools. In terms of security, it adds cryptographic authentication in order to prevent various man-in-the-middle attacks, notably eavesdropping and malicious hashrate redirection. An important aspect of Stratum V2 is that it includes sub-protocols allowing individual miners to choose their own sets of transactions to include in the blocks they work on. This feature gives more power to individual miners, unlike the original protocol where pools had full control over the *block template*. This method would thus strengthen the decentralization of the mining process by pools.

entries.title: STUCKLESS PAYMENT
entries.body:
A proposal to solve the problem of stuck payments on the Lightning Network. With current HTLCs, a payment can remain stuck without being either completed or canceled, for example if an intermediate node goes offline or deliberately holds the HTLC. The sender must then wait for the *timelock* to expire to recover their funds, and cannot retry the same payment without risking paying the recipient twice.

*Stuckless payments*, proposed by Hiroki Gondo, are based on PTLCs and add an extra round of communication between the sender and the recipient when the payment is set up and settled. This mechanism introduces a confirmation key (*acknowledgment key*) that the sender controls: the recipient can only finalize the payment after receiving this key. The sender can thus launch several attempts in parallel over different routes, with the guarantee that if one succeeds, all the others will automatically fail. This eliminates the risk of double payment and improves routing reliability on Lightning.

entries.title: SUBMARINE SWAP
entries.body:
An atomic exchange between on-chain bitcoins and off-chain bitcoins on the Lightning Network, without counterparty risk. Neither party takes *custody* of the other's funds: either the exchange succeeds in full, or it fails and each party recovers their funds.

The mechanism relies on the same HTLCs (*Hash Time-Locked Contracts*) as those used in Lightning routing. The recipient of the Lightning payment generates a secret preimage whose hash is used to build both an on-chain contract and an off-chain payment. The on-chain payer locks their bitcoins in a conditional script: the funds can be claimed by the recipient if they provide the preimage and their signature, or recovered by the payer after the *timelock* expires. When the Lightning payment is made, the preimage is revealed, which allows the recipient to claim the on-chain funds.

entries.title: SWAP-IN POTENTIAM
entries.body:
A protocol that makes it possible to transfer on-chain bitcoins to the Lightning Network almost instantly, without relying on 0-conf channels. Proposed by Jesse Posner and ZmnSCPxj in 2023, it relies on an on-chain address shared between the user (Alice) and an LSP (Bob).

This address encodes two spending paths: a cooperative path, where Alice and Bob jointly sign to move the funds, and a unilateral recovery path, where Alice can take back her bitcoins after a *timelock* expires. When funds are received and confirmed at this address, Alice can, with the help of the LSP, immediately move them into an existing or new Lightning channel, via the cooperative path. If the LSP is unavailable, Alice retains the ability to recover her funds on-chain after the specified delay.

The main advantage of *Swap-in Potentiam* is that it reduces trust requirements compared with other methods of instantly opening channels. The temporary co-ownership of the funds and the security *timelock* ensure that neither Alice nor the LSP can steal the funds. The Phoenix wallet from the company ACINQ uses a variant of this protocol called “Swaproot,” adapted to the constraints of mobile devices with intermittent connectivity.

entries.title: SWAPROOT
entries.body:
An on-chain deposit protocol to a Lightning channel designed by ACINQ and deployed in the Phoenix wallet in February 2024. Swaproot is an evolution of the *swap-in potentiam* protocol that leverages Taproot and MuSig2 to make swap-in transactions cheaper, more private and compatible with address rotation.

The old protocol used a *pay-to-script* construction of the form “user key + server key OR user key + delay.” This structure was identifiable on-chain and required a static address. Swaproot replaces the cooperative path with a Taproot *key-path* spend: the user's and the server's keys are aggregated via MuSig2 into a single public key. When both parties cooperate to perform a *splice-in*, the transaction is indistinguishable from an ordinary P2TR payment. The refund path (user key + delay) is relegated to the *script-path*, invisible except in the case of unilateral recovery.

entries.title: SWEEP TRANSACTION
entries.body:
A *pattern*, or transaction template, used in chain analysis to determine the nature of the transaction. This pattern is characterized by the consumption of a single UTXO as input and the production of a single UTXO as output. The interpretation of this pattern is that we are looking at a self-transfer. The user transferred their bitcoins to themselves, to another address belonging to them. Since there is no change on the transaction, it is very unlikely that we are looking at a payment. Indeed, when a payment is made, it is almost impossible for the payer to have a UTXO that matches exactly the amount required by the seller, plus the transaction fees. In general, the payer is therefore obliged to produce a change output. We then know that the observed user probably still holds this UTXO. In chain analysis, if we know that the UTXO used as the transaction's input belongs to Alice, we can assume that the output UTXO also belongs to her.

![Sweep transaction: a single UTXO of 50,000 sats as input and a single output of 49,000 sats, the signature of a self-transfer.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/LoicPandul/Dictionnaire-de-Bitcoin/bab568e32351cc9f1240f49f5feedc242123d101/definitions/fr/s/sweep-transaction/assets/image-1.png)

entries.title: SWISS BITCOIN PAY
entries.body:
A Bitcoin payment terminal solution intended for merchants and businesses. Swiss Bitcoin Pay makes it possible to accept bitcoin payments, both *on-chain* and via the Lightning Network, through a mobile application or an API that can be integrated into existing point-of-sale systems.

The service operates on a hybrid model: it facilitates receiving payments without the merchant needing to manage a node or technical infrastructure themselves, and then it automatically pays out the takings every day. The funds received can be kept in bitcoins, automatically converted into fiat currency, or a *mix* of the two, depending on the merchant's preferences.

Swiss Bitcoin Pay positions itself between fully self-hosted solutions like BTCPay Server and *custodian* payment processors, and offers a compromise between ease of use and sovereignty over funds.

entries.title: SYBIL
entries.body: A computer attack in which an individual or entity creates multiple false identities in a system in order to exert undue influence or gain an unauthorized advantage. In the context of Bitcoin, such an attack aims to gain undue influence over the system, thereby making it possible to manipulate the consensus mechanisms. To counter Sybil attacks, Satoshi Nakamoto devised a proof-of-work system that imposes a non-negligible marginal cost on the creation of multiple votes.

entries.title: SYNONYM
entries.body: A technology company founded by John Carvalho, focused on developing software and protocols that promote a peer-to-peer economy centered on Bitcoin. Synonym is the originator of the Slashtags protocol, a decentralized web standard that makes it possible to derive additional key pairs from a BIP-0039 seed in order to create profiles, contacts and passwordless authentication. The company also developed Bitkit, a mobile wallet with an embedded Lightning node.

entries.title: UNECONOMICAL OUTPUT
entries.body:
Refers to extremely small amounts of bitcoin coins that are too tiny to be sent in a transaction, because the fees needed to include them in a block would be proportionally higher than their value. The precise definition of "dust" may vary depending on the context, but it is generally any transaction output that requires more fees to be spent than the value it embodies. For the Bitcoin user, it is important to manage their UTXOs, and to practice consolidating them, so that they do not become dust.

*In English, the term "uneconomical outputs" is sometimes encountered to refer to dust.*
